# Dasarathajātaka (Ja 461)

**ID:** Ja 461
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Dasarathajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** King Dasaratha
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja461

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dasarathajātaka* (Ja 461) is the Buddhist adaptation of the Rāma legend in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010; Holt 2008]. In the frame story set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the tale to comfort a grief-stricken householder mourning the death of his father by demonstrating that wise men of old bore loss without sorrow [SuttaCentral; Winternitz 1933]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as Rāmapaṇḍita, son of King Dasaratha of Benares, alongside his brother Lakkhaṇa and sister Sītā [Holt 2008; Huynh 2016]. Following palace intrigues after the king grants a boon to a younger queen for her son Bharata, Rāma, Lakkhaṇa, and Sītā withdraw to the forest [Anālayo 2010; Holt 2008; Huynh 2016]. When King Dasaratha dies, Bharata seeks Rāma in exile, but Rāma refuses to return until his father's designated term is complete, granting his straw slippers to rule in his stead; at the conclusion, Rāma returns to reign with Sītā as his queen consort [Holt 2008; Huynh 2016]. Notably, the narrative omits the abduction of Sītā and the expedition to Laṅkā found in the classical Sanskrit epic [Eliot 1921; Holt 2008]. Scholars note that the canonical verses (*gāthā*) essentially comprise moral sayings on impermanence to console the bereaved rather than an epic narrative, the latter being elaborated in the prose commentary [Winternitz 1933; Appleton 2010].

Verses from the *Dasarathajātaka* share substantial thematic and textual parallels across Buddhist canonical literature. Curated parallels exist with the *Salla Sutta* (Snp 3.8), the *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538), several Dharmapada and Udānavarga traditions including the Gāndhārī Dharmapada (G-Dhp 139–161, G3-Dhp 41–50), the Sanskrit Udānavarga (UV 1), and Chinese translations (T 210, T 212, and T 213) [SuttaCentral]. Computational text-reuse analysis confirms substantial overlap between Ja 461 and Snp 3.8, as well as extensive reproduction in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo), alongside alignments with Tibetan canonical works such as the *Rājadeśa-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra* (D0214) and Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (D3940) [DharmaNexus].

**Sources**

- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text-reuse matches for Ja 461 — Pali-internal matches with Snp 3.8 and the Jātaka commentary, and Tibetan cross-language alignments.
